effect: Hobbes’s account connects authorized sovereign power to peace, setting up the question of what happens when protection fails.
reaction: The caveat that concentrated power may fail is useful.
reason: Test the stated limit of obedience against a sovereign’s failure to protect.
expectation: I expect Hobbes’s account of whether the subject still owes obedience when protection is no longer possible.

effect: Hobbes’s protection-based limit is clear; I’ll turn to Locke’s account of consent.
reaction: The distinction between lost protection and merely disliking a decision is useful.
reason: This is the only offered combination and begins the remaining Locke goal.

reason: This is the only offered combination and addresses the remaining goal about breach of trust.

effect: Locke’s account makes arbitrary seizure a breach of trust that can justify resistance, distinct from Hobbes’s protection-based limit.
reaction: The concrete harvest example clarifies the distinction, and the caveat about resistance not necessarily succeeding is useful.

mostWorthwhile.text: Testing Locke’s account against arbitrary seizure was most worthwhile: the harvest example made the breach of trust concrete.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial statement that authorized sovereign power can secure peace felt broad compared with the more specific test that followed.

surprise.text: Hobbes’s account allows a subject’s duty to end when protection is lost, rather than treating obedience as unconditional.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the fast menu made the later choices effectively automatic rather than discoveries of compatibility.

continue.text: I would continue: comparing the two limits on authority was concise and raised useful distinctions, even if the choices became automatic.
